summary: Children learn to read rock strata as a record of time: layers build up with the oldest at the bottom (superposition, which holds for layers that have not been folded, overturned or otherwise disturbed), and fossils in different layers are evidence of organisms that lived at different times, so patterns in the rock reveal how a landscape changed over long periods. The focus is the evidence-reading inference — ordering events and reconstructing landscape change from layers and fossils — kept to RELATIVE time (older/younger, before/after), never absolute dates or the detailed mechanism of rock formation.
misconceptions: All rock layers formed at the same time, or the order of layers does not indicate time.
The youngest/oldest layer is at the top (reversing superposition).
Fossils are only dinosaur bones, or are just 'pictures in rocks', rather than remains of once-living organisms.
You can read the exact age of a layer directly by looking at it (confusing relative with absolute dating).
Landscapes are fixed — rather than the product of change recorded in the layers.

activities.title: Build-up-the-layers time machine
steps: Deposit sediment one layer at a time as 'time' passes, so each new layer settles on top of the last.
In each era, place/bury an organism in the layer being formed at that time (e.g. a trilobite early, an ammonite later).
Relate the build-up to a jar: pour in sand, then mud, then gravel, letting each settle before adding the next — the first poured ends up at the bottom, mirroring how the oldest layer sits lowest.
Cut into the resulting cliff/cross-section and read it back: order the buried fossils from earliest-lived to latest-lived.
State, in your own words, why the fossil in the lower layer must be older than the one above it.
Reconstruct how the landscape changed over time from the sequence of layers and the fossils in them.
activities.insight: The trilobite resting at the BOTTOM must be older than the ammonite above it, because its layer was deposited — and the organism buried — first. Undisturbed rock layers are a stack of time with the oldest underneath, so a landscape's history can be read from its layers.

activities.title: Read real strata and reconstruct the story
steps: Examine a real, dramatic strata cross-section (a canyon wall or cliff face) with many visible layers that are flat-lying and not folded or overturned.
Identify which layers are older and younger using the oldest-at-the-bottom rule.
Match named fossils to the layers they appear in and order the organisms by relative time.
Write or say a short explanation of how this landscape changed over a long time, citing the layer/fossil pattern as evidence.
Transfer the reasoning to a second, unfamiliar cliff with undisturbed layers to check you can apply the rule to new evidence.
activities.insight: The ordering rule applies to genuine evidence: real rock formations whose layers have not been overturned record a sequence of events, and you can construct the landscape's history from the pattern of layers and fossils rather than memorising a told story.

activities.title: Labelled strata cross-section reference
steps: Study a labelled strata cross-section with the oldest layer at the bottom.
Reveal, for a selected layer or fossil, its relative age and which organism it represents (e.g. tap or lift a panel).
Use it to check vocabulary: sediment, strata, fossil, layer.
activities.insight: A clear reference links each layer and fossil to its relative position and age, anchoring the vocabulary used when reasoning about order.

activities.title: Sequence and match check
steps: Order a set of layers from oldest to youngest.
Match each named fossil to the layer it belongs in.
Answer a short reasoning question on superposition, e.g. which of two fossils lived earlier and why.
Explain WHY, not just WHICH, so the rule you are using is visible.
activities.insight: Ordering and matching reveal whether the learner is applying superposition correctly and connecting fossil position to time, or using an inverted/single-event rule.

checkQuestion: In a cliff face you find a trilobite fossil in a low layer and an ammonite fossil in a higher layer. Which animal lived earlier — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: The trilobite, in the lower layer, lived earlier: rock layers build up over time with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest on top, so a fossil in a lower layer was buried longer ago.
